what_its_for: Oxaliplatin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat colon and rectal cancer. It is often given along with other chemotherapy drugs to help stop cancer cells from growing and spreading in your body.
how_to_take: Oxaliplatin is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor at a cancer treatment center or hospital. You will NOT take this medicine as a pill at home. Each infusion usually takes about 2 to 6 hours. You will receive this treatment in cycles, meaning you get treatment on certain days followed by rest days to let your body recover.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your exact dose based on your height and weight (called body surface area). A common schedule is receiving an infusion once every 2 weeks. Never try to adjust your dose on your own. Always follow your oncologist's (cancer doctor's) instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital, missed doses are handled by your medical team. If you need to reschedule or miss an appointment, call your cancer care team as soon as possible so they can find the best time to reschedule your treatment. Do not skip treatments without talking to your doctor first.
storage: Oxaliplatin is stored and prepared by pharmacy professionals at the treatment center — you do not need to store this medicine at home. The prepared IV solution must be kept refrigerated and used within a specific time frame as directed by the pharmacy.
what_to_avoid: Avoid cold temperatures, cold drinks, and cold food during treatment and for several days after each infusion, as cold can trigger or worsen painful nerve tingling or numbness in your hands, feet, and throat. Do not hold cold objects, drink cold beverages, or go outside in cold weather without wearing gloves and warm clothing. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not receive any vaccines (especially live vaccines) without asking your doctor first. Avoid contact with people who are sick, as your immune system may be weakened. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or have vision problems.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: trouble breathing, swallowing, or speaking; sudden severe allergic reaction (hives, swelling of the face or throat, rapid heartbeat, dizziness); severe numbness, tingling, or pain in your hands or feet that does not go away; signs of infection such as fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or unusual weakness; unusual bleeding or bruising; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; dark or bloody stools; yellowing of your skin or eyes; or significant chest pain.
when_it_works: Oxaliplatin begins working right away at the cellular level with each infusion, but you may not see or feel results immediately. Your doctor will monitor your progress through regular blood tests, scans, and check-ups over several weeks or months to see how well the treatment is working. It is important to complete all scheduled cycles of treatment even if you feel well.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. If your kidneys are not working well, your dose may need to be adjusted or treatment may need to be delayed. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Oxaliplatin can harm an unborn baby. You must use effective birth control during treatment and for several months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Fertility: This medicine may affect fertility in both men and women. Talk to your doctor about your options before starting treatment. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, especially nerve-related side effects (neuropathy). Your doctor will monitor you closely.
